lessons.title: The Five Stages of a Crisis: From Boom to Recovery

body.text: From the inside, every crisis feels like chaos. From a distance, almost every one follows the same five-act script: build-up, trigger, panic, response, repair.

children.text: In March 2014, Indian banks reported gross bad loans of 3.8% of their total lending. By March 2018, that figure had nearly tripled to 11.2%, and at public sector banks it touched 14.58%. By March 2026, it had fallen to about 1.8%, a multi-decade low. That is a complete crisis cycle, played out over twelve years, in the banks most Indians keep their savings in. Most investors only noticed it in the middle.
This lesson gives you the five-stage map. Every crisis in the rest of this course will be walked through using it, so you always know where you are in the story.

body.title: The five stages of a financial crisis

events.title: Build-up
events.description: Credit grows faster than the economy. Lending standards loosen, asset prices rise, and success makes everyone more willing to borrow and lend.

events.title: Trigger
events.description: A shock, often small, exposes the weakness: a default, a rate hike, an oil price spike, a failed auction, or a sudden policy change.

events.title: Panic and recognition
events.description: Confidence breaks. Lenders pull back, asset prices fall, and hidden losses are finally recognised. Contagion spreads the damage.

events.title: Policy response
events.description: Central banks, governments and sometimes the IMF step in with cash, guarantees, rate cuts and bailouts to stop the spiral.

events.title: Repair and recovery
events.description: Bad loans are written off, balance sheets are rebuilt, rules are rewritten, and growth slowly returns. This stage usually lasts years.

children.text: Stage 1: Build-up
Every crisis begins as a success story. A new technology, a property boom, a reform, or a flood of foreign money makes lending look safe and profitable. This is a
credit boom
. Borrowers take on more debt because asset prices keep rising, and lenders lend more because borrowers keep repaying.

markDefs.definition: A period when lending grows much faster than the economy, usually accompanied by looser lending standards and rising asset prices.

children.text: India's version ran through the mid to late 2000s. Banks, especially public sector banks, lent heavily to infrastructure, power, steel and telecom projects on the assumption that the high growth of those years would continue.

body.text: The build-up is the only stage where prevention is cheap, and it is also the stage where nobody wants to hear warnings. Rising prices make the risk look like proof of safety.

children.text: Stage 2: Trigger
The trigger is rarely the cause. It is the moment the market is forced to look at a weakness that was already there. Classic triggers include:
A large default, like Lehman Brothers in September 2008 or IL&FS in September 2018
A central bank raising rates or signalling it will pull back support, like the US Fed in May 2013
An oil price shock, like the Gulf War spike in 1990 that drained India's dollar reserves
A regulator forcing honest accounting, like the RBI's Asset Quality Review in 2015
Stage 3: Panic and Recognition

Once the trigger hits, losses that were hidden or ignored start being recognised. Lenders stop rolling over debt, asset prices fall, and contagion carries the damage outward, exactly as Lesson 2 described.
Not every crisis has a dramatic, one-week panic. India's bad loan crisis was a slow-motion version. For years, many stressed loans were kept looking healthy through
evergreening
. The RBI's Asset Quality Review in 2015 forced banks to classify these loans honestly, and reported bad loans jumped by around 80% in 2015-16 alone.

markDefs.definition: Giving a struggling borrower fresh loans so it can pay interest on old ones, which keeps the original loan from being classified as bad even though the borrower cannot actually repay.

body.title: Show me how evergreening hides a bad loan

children.text: A steel company owes a bank ₹1,000 crore and must pay ₹100 crore of interest this year. Its plant is running at a loss, so it has no cash to pay.

headers: How the loan looks on the bank's books

cells: Honest recognition
Interest is missed for more than 90 days
Classified as a non-performing asset; the bank must set aside money to cover the likely loss
Evergreening
The bank lends another ₹100 crore, which the company uses to pay the interest
Looks like a healthy, paying loan, but total debt is now ₹1,100 crore

children.text: Evergreening does not remove the loss. It delays it and makes it bigger, because the unpayable debt keeps growing. That is why the recognition stage, when it finally comes, feels so sudden.

body.title: Calculate the Gross NPA Ratio
body.prompt: A bank has gross advances (total loans) of ₹4,00,000 crore. Of these, ₹44,800 crore are classified as non-performing assets. What is its gross NPA ratio, in %?
body.explanation: Gross NPA ratio = Gross NPAs ÷ Gross advances × 100 = ₹44,800 crore ÷ ₹4,00,000 crore × 100 = 11.2%. That happens to match the peak for all Indian scheduled commercial banks in March 2018.

children.text: Stage 4: Policy Response

At this point, private players cannot stop the spiral on their own, because everyone is hoarding cash at the same time. Only the state has the balance sheet to break the freeze. The central bank acts as the
lender of last resort
, and the government decides who gets rescued and who takes the loss.

markDefs.definition: A central bank's role of lending cash to sound but illiquid banks during a panic, when no private lender will, to stop a liquidity crisis from turning into a wave of failures.

body.caption: The policy toolkit, and how India has used it

cells: Liquidity injection
Floods banks with cash so they keep lending
RBI cut the CRR from 9% to 5% between October 2008 and January 2009
Emergency rescue of a failing firm
Replaces management and stops disorderly collapse
Government took control of the IL&FS board on 1 October 2018
Bank recapitalisation
Injects fresh capital so banks can absorb losses
₹2.11 lakh crore plan for public sector banks, announced October 2017
New resolution framework
Creates a faster way to deal with defaulters
Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016
Emergency foreign currency
Raises dollars for a country that has run out of reserves
IMF loan plus 67 tonnes of gold pledged to raise dollars in 1991

body.title: Name the Role
body.textWithBlank: When the RBI lends cash to banks during a panic because no private lender will, it is acting as the lender of last ___.
body.explanation: Lender of last resort. The idea is to save banks that are illiquid but fundamentally sound, before a shortage of cash turns into real failures.

children.text: Stage 5: Repair and Recovery

This is the longest and least dramatic stage. Banks write off bad loans and rebuild capital. Borrowers sell assets and cut debt. Regulators rewrite the rules that failed. Growth returns, but slowly, because households, companies and banks are all busy repairing their balance sheets instead of spending and lending.
Economists Carmen Reinhart and Kenneth Rogoff studied major banking crises and measured how deep the aftermath typically runs.

children.text: The chart shows the full arc of India's cycle. Recognition drove the ratio up to 2018. The response, through recapitalisation, the IBC and years of write-offs and recoveries, then brought it down. Notice that the climb took about four years, and the full repair took around eight.

body.title: Which Stage Is This?
body.question: In October 2008, weeks after Lehman failed, the RBI began cutting the cash reserve ratio to release liquidity into Indian banks. Which stage does this action belong to?
body.explanation: This is policy response. The trigger (Lehman) and the panic (frozen credit markets, rumours about ICICI Bank) had already happened. Cutting the CRR is the central bank using its toolkit to stop the spiral.

body.title: Place Today's Headlines on the Map
body.scenario: Imagine you read these three headlines in the same month. One: "Unsecured personal loans have grown more than twice as fast as overall bank credit for three years." Two: "Lenders report falling defaults and record profits." Three: "Regulator raises capital requirements on unsecured consumer loans."
body.prompt: Which stage do these signals most resemble, what might a trigger look like, and why is the regulator acting when defaults are low?
body.modelAnswer: These signals most resemble Stage 1, build-up. Credit in one segment is growing far faster than the economy, while low defaults and record profits make the lending look safe. That is the classic build-up pattern: success hides the risk. A trigger could be a rise in interest rates that squeezes borrowers, a wave of job losses, or the failure of a lender heavily concentrated in that segment. The regulator acts while defaults are low because the build-up is the only stage where prevention is cheap. Once defaults start rising, it is already Stage 3, and the cost of fixing the problem is far higher. Note that a build-up does not guarantee a crisis. It means the risk is rising, which is exactly when careful investors start checking concentration and asset quality instead of relying on recent profits.

cards.definition: Credit grows faster than the economy, standards loosen, and rising asset prices make risk look safe.
The shock that forces the market to confront a weakness already in place. Rarely the real cause.
Confidence breaks, hidden losses are recognised, and contagion spreads the damage.
Central banks and governments use liquidity, guarantees, bailouts and rate cuts to stop the spiral.
Losses are written off, balance sheets and rules are rebuilt, and growth returns slowly over years.
Lending fresh money to a struggling borrower so it can pay interest on old loans, hiding the bad loan.

body.label: RBI Financial Stability Report
body.description: Published twice a year, in June and December. It reports bank bad loan ratios, capital levels and the RBI's own view of emerging risks, which makes it the best single place to judge which stage India's financial system is in.

points: Most financial crises follow five stages: build-up, trigger, panic and recognition, policy response, and repair and recovery
The trigger is rarely the cause; it exposes a weakness that built up during the boom
Some crises are slow-motion, like India's bad loan cycle, where evergreening delayed recognition for years
The state is usually the only actor that can end the panic, through liquidity, recapitalisation, new resolution laws or IMF support
Repair takes years: Indian banks' gross NPA ratio took about four years to peak at 11.2% and around eight more to fall to about 1.8%

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute investment advice. The headlines in the scenario exercise are hypothetical. Figures are drawn from public RBI, government and academic sources believed accurate at the time of writing.
